Based on analyses of new seismic proﬁles and multi-beam bathymetric data, this paper analyzes MTDs in detail and discusses triggering mechanism of MTDs of the northern South China Sea. 2 REGIONAL GEOLOGICAL SETTING Three large deepwater basins, the Qiongdongnan basin, Pearl River Mouth basin and Taixinan basin, are distributed from west to east along the northern South China Sea margin (Fig. 1). Geological structure in the margin is very complex[11]. The northern slope of the South China Sea margin exhibits NE vergence and becomes gradually narrow from east to west, and the average water depth of this area is about 1100 m[12]. Steep and gentle slopes in the continental margin are in an alternating arrangement. The submarine terrain from west to east is ladder-like drop, and the dividing line between continental slope and deep-sea plains is from 3300 m to 3700 m. The average gradient of slope is 10 times or even more than that of continental shelf[13]. The continental slope across the Xisha Islands area and Zhongshan Islands area of the northwest margin is relatively broad (water depth from 800 m to 1600 m), and the region with water depth > 1600 m of the slope becomes steeper sharply. The slope in the Qiongdongnan basin with striking of NE is located along the east-westernward Xisha trough, south of Hainan Island and east of the Yinggehai basin. The north continental slope in the Qiongdongnan basin began to develop mainly along traces of large faults in the late Miocene, and initially developed in the east part of the basin. Some wide valleys and gravity ﬂow deposits can be found in this area[13]. The north continental slope in the Qiongdongnan basin can be divided into three sections: (1) The west part: in this section,

It covers about 17.5×104 km2 of which total depressions are about 10.9×104 km2, whereas uplifts are about 6.6×104 km2. The deepwater depressions are dominated in the Zhu II sag. The continental slope topography in this basin is quite complicated. The slope is of NE trend in the west and changes into NEE or EW trend in the east. As a rifted basin it is composed of a series of half-grabens. The terrain in the basin decreases from east to west, and rises in northern and falls in southern. The upper slope is typically gentle while the lower slope is steep (with slope gradient about 3◦). Tens of submarine canyons developed well from west to east. Mass of epicontinental sediments transported to deep-water environment by gravity ﬂow, and in the south of these canyons formed large-scale MTDs more than 10000 km2. The Taixinan basin is located in the northeast of the South China Sea. It covers continental shelf, continental slope and deep sea plain. A series of large-scale submarine canyons are present in the Taiwan shoal near the shelf break zone, and in this area volumes of MTDs can be discovered. 3 DEPOSITIONAL STRUCTURES AND SEISMIC CHARACTERISTICS OF MTDs MTDs are one kind of processes driven by gravity ﬂows. They often appear in the marine strata because large volumes of sediments can be transported in a short period[19], and these sediments can be distinguished from around normal sediments clearly using multi-beam bathymetric data and seismic sections. Usually a series of long strip grooves formed along the upper zone, and this is one of potential symbols of submarine slope failure (Fig. 2a, Fig. 3). 3.1 Headwall Scarps Headwall scarps are sediments tensioned by gravity and then deformation or even failure occurs while the shear force exceeds a certain value (Fig. 2). Each headwall scarp shows an arcuate feature, and its width varies between 5 km to 8 km with the maximum about 17 km in the slope of the Qiongdongnan basin. A set of typical and large-scale Quaternary MTDs developed in the Baiyun sag of the Pearl River Mouth basin (Fig. 2a), where the maximum width of headwall scarps is 16.5 km, and the water depth of this region is over 1100 m. Numerous MTDs developed in the Taixinan basin are usually of small scales, which are distributed mainly at 300 m to 500 m water depths, most of which have widths less than 3 km. 3.2 Side Scarps Lateral margins are the dip-parallel side boundaries of MTDs, which are parallel to the ﬂow direction. Lateral margins are associated with strike-slip movement, where strata are eroded. In a platform, lateral scarps may exhibit a linear feature roughly parallel to the slope direction which separates a smooth, undeformed region of the seabed from the adjacent region that has been aﬀected by failure (Fig. 2a, Fig. 3). The identiﬁcation of lateral scarps can be of great value to the kinematic study of MTDs, as they oﬀer a primary constraint on the ﬂow direction of the MTDs and can help to conﬁrm the side limits. MTD features between both lateral margins that are conspicuous features in seismic slices; generally they are chaotic and can be distinguished from un-failure seabed obviously. Lateral scarps in the slope of the Qiongdongnan basin can be recognized clearly in general, and that of the western part is diﬃcult to identify where the water depth is over 1200 m. Lateral scarps of the Pearl River Mouth basin are very typical, in plane view the length of northern lateral scarp is about 208 km, and the southern one is about 130 km long. 3.3 Top Surfaces Top surfaces of MTDs are complex units, which tend to preserve information related to the deposition and cessation of events. Sediments are deformed seriously during the transport process, which may be reformed by channel or bottom current and then the top surface of MTDs was gradually reshaped as irregular morphology, and these features can be reﬂected by seismic slices and multi-beam images. Geophys. Vol.54, No.6 4 DISTRIBUTION OF MTDS MTDs are widely distributed in the shallow strata of the northern South China Sea. Based on the interpretation of the multi-beam bathymetry data and seismic sections, we found there are 4 large-scale MTDs (Fig. 7): (1) the northern slope of the Qiongdongnan basin (named Qiongbei MTDs); (2) the southern part of the Qiongdongnan basin (named Huaguang MTDs); (3) Baiyun MTDs of the Pearl Mouth River basin; and (4) Jiulong MTDs of the Taixinan basin. Qiongbei MTDs distributed in the upslope between 110◦18′ to 111◦42′E cover an area about 13000 km2, and the scale of single MTDs increases from west to east (headwall area increases to 180 km2 from 40 km2). Erosion depth gradually deepens to 620 m from 150 m, and the shape tends to be complicated. MTDs in this area are mostly controlled by the slope gradient (the western part with smaller gradient, mainly < 10◦ while the eastern part always > 12◦). We inferred that the Qiongbei MTDs have close relationship with submarine morphology, frequent sea-level changes and high deposition rate. Huaguang MTDs occur in the Huangliu Formation and Quaternary strata, southeastern of the Qiongdong- nan basin with the total area about 16000 km2. The transport direction is NW-SE, which is because sediments are transported from low position to high position, and many synsedimentary thrust faults can be identiﬁed in this area. According to tectonic settings, Huaguang MTDs are closely associated with the tectonic reversion of fault zones in the west of the South China Sea 5 Ma ago. Baiyun MTDs are mainly located in the Zhu II sag, the northern part develop several submarine channels, and both ﬂanks are distributed plenty of MTDs. In the southern part there developed large scale MTDs which cover an area over 13000 km2. Slope gradient of Baiyun MTDs area is between 1◦ to 14.5◦, of which the upper zone has typical structures, such as extensional blocks, headwall scarps and lateral scarps. Seismic facies include blocky parallel, undulated structure and chaotic reﬂection. Baiyun MTDs have close relationship with gas hydrate dissolution and high pressure of strata. Jiulong MTDs are situated in the slope of the northeastern part of the South China Sea with the total area about 11000 km2. MTDs on east and west sides are greater than the middle part, and erosion depth also gradually deepens from both sides to the middle area. In the down slope area, compressional structures can be recognized obviously. Jiulong MTDs are closely associated with earthquakes, bottom current and dissolution of gas hydrate. It expresses stability before slide. However, it becomes instable when sediment strength decreases or the shear stress increases continuously. At ﬁrst, deformation and tiny slide occur when the shear stress is over the shear strength. Afterwards by the persistent deformation, the interrupt extensional faults developed. With increasing scale of the faulting, and coupled with other factors, the total sedimentary layers are instable, and MTDs formed[1∼4,21]. For the time being, initial development and dynamic sedimentary processes are still problematic. It is a focused subject for many scientists[21]. In this paper we just discuss inﬂuence factors at the initial development. The triggering factors of MTDs include following aspects: earthquakes, gas hydrate dissolution, tectonic induced steep slope angle, high rapid sedimentary rate and sea level change[21∼24]. The MTDs in the northern slope of the SCS show diﬀerent generations. We consider that gas hydrate dissolution, sea level change and high rapid sedimentary supply could be important factors for generation of MTDs in the northern SCS[25]. We will discuss the mechanism of the Baiyun MTDs below. 5.1 Gas Hydrate Dissolution with MTDs In the Pearl River Mouth basin, Baiyun MTDs are located in the Baiyun sag where the LW3-1-1 big gas ﬁeld lies. In 2007, China achieved successfully gas hydrated samples in the region. In recent years, the investigation shows that the Baiyun sag is the most important prospective area of gas hydrate in our country[25]. The formation and dissolution of gas hydrate have a very close relationship with the formation of MTDs. From Fig. 8, gas hydrate bottom is consistent with the bottom of MTDs. When gas hydrate dissolution occurs, it can release much water and free gas. The process of solid material transforming into liquid and gas hydrate reduces the shear strength of sediment, which makes the sediment more vulnerable to damage. When

From Fig. 8, gas hydrate bottom is consistent with the bottom of MTDs. When gas hydrate dissolution occurs, it can release much water and free gas. The process of solid material transforming into liquid and gas hydrate reduces the shear strength of sediment, which makes the sediment more vulnerable to damage. When a layer of weakness forms between the sedimentary formations, it is likely to cause the Baiyun MTDs. Secondly, gas hydrate dissolution process also enhances the pore pressure of sediments. When the gas in the pores reaches saturation, gas hydrate dissolution will continue to release the water and gas into the pores, the volume of which will exceed the original volume of gas hydrate. When it is in a well closed environment, the pressure of strata will increase. Gas hydrate dissolution can lead to excess pressure and cause formation stress gather, which results in developing MTDs in the stress concentrating area. 5.2 Numerical Simulation 5.2.1 Numerical calculation model By analyzing the inﬂuences of submarine slope geological environment and gas hydrates dissolution, it can be seen that the factors such as geometric shape of submarine slope, thickness of sediment and gas hydrate zone, and geometric shape of gas hydrate zone have certain eﬀects on the submarine slope from geometric characteristics of slope. Therefore, we have collated and integrated new as well as published data for both the formerly glaciated and non-glaciated areas of this highly dynamic margin for a time period mainly from the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) to the present. Mass transport type is predominantly translational sliding on the high-latitude continental margins (north of 52�N), whereas turbidites dominate on lower latitudes. This is partly related to the average slope of the respective continental margin segments and differences in both sediment types and soil properties. Additionally, on low latitudes, submarine slope failures mainly occurred during glacial conditions with low sea level, whereas on high latitudes, they occur during the relatively fast transition from glacial to interglacial conditions (i.e. during periods of sea level rise). Introduction The aim of this study is to present and discuss the large variety of mass wasting processes on glaciated and non-glaciated continental margins of the NE-Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Seas in rela- tion to seismic hazards, sediment properties, and sea level changes. The assessment of today’s submarine continental slope stability requires an understanding of what has caused submarine slope failures in the past. Knowledge of preconditions of sediments to fail and their triggering mechanisms has improved signiﬁcantly following extensive studies conducted throughout the world. Particularly the multidisciplinary investigations and interactions between academia and industry in studying the giant Storegga Slide complex of the mid-Norwegian margin have revealed new insights into the occurrence and dynamics of mass wasting in relation to sedimentation and oceanographic processes, glacial history and seismicity, which together form a key study for slope failure on (formerly) glaciated margins (e.g. Mienert, 2004; Bryn et al., 2005a; Solheim et al., 2005a, b). Potential preconditions to failure exist in the form of weak sediment layers, and they have been used to explain the architecture of the Storegga Slide (Bryn et al., 2003). However, the absence of other large (regional) scale slope failures in similar geological settings is difﬁcult to under- stand, and we need to shed more light on such complex, interacting processes. In order to gather more information about the key parameters controlling sediment instabilities on continental margins, it is essential to study both the spatial distribution and the frequency of submarine slides (e.g., McAdoo et al., 2000;Canals et al., 2004b; Mienert, 2004). Instabilities on continental margins are of interest not only for the understanding of sedimentary processes building or removing strata but also for estimatingdand ultimately elimi- natingdrisks related to failure impacts on offshore infrastructure and coastal communities (e.g. tsunami generation). Mega-size (sediment volume >1000 km3) sediment slides appear to be concentrated on the formerly glaciated margins of the NE-Atlantic, extending over several hundreds of km on the mid-Norwegian margin (e.g. the Storegga Slide, Haﬂidason et al., 2004) and the Arctic margin north of Svalbard (Vanneste et al., 2006; Winklemann et al., 2006). One of the characteristics and development mechanism for slope failure on glaciated margins is retrogressive sliding; however, one should not ignore (glacial and non-glacial) debris ﬂows, turbidites and megaturbidites. All these speciﬁc sedimentary processes affect the continental margin morphology and sub-seaﬂoor character from the shelf break and upper slope to the deep ocean basins. These processes lead to a diversity of seismic signatures from chaotic sediment depocentres to well-stratiﬁed layers, sedimentary scarps and sediment pressure ridges, which are in turn partly draped or inﬁlled by contourite drifts, related to well-established oceano- graphic circulation patterns (e.g. Laberg and Vorren, 2003a; Canals et al., 2004a; Haﬂidason et al., 2004; Solheim et al., 2005a). A variety of mechanisms can initiate submarine mass movement (Sultan et al., 2004a). For example, the rapid deformation of sedi- ments affecting the stress–strain relationship could lead to sediment failure, whereas a more progressive deformation of sediments may allow a change in soil properties and shear strength leading to strain softening and creeping. For example, the rapid deformation of sedi- ments affecting the stress–strain relationship could lead to sediment failure, whereas a more progressive deformation of sediments may allow a change in soil properties and shear strength leading to strain softening and creeping. Among the potential triggers and destabilization processes, the most relevant are high sedimentation rates, climatically-controlled alternations in sedi- mentation, gas hydrate dissociation in the sediment’s pore space, diapirism, uplift and earthquakes, which would all lead to excess pore pressure development and consequently reduction of shear strength (Bryn et al., 2005a). Using a recent compilation of submarine mass movements on European continental margins, we try to highlight their genesis mechanisms at a large-scale (Atlantic and Mediterranean) to emphasize similarities between mass wasting events occurring in closed areas and thus propose some models regarding likely recurrent processes at regional scales. 2. The non-glaciated margin is further subdivided. The ﬁrst area lies between 52�N and 35�N and the margin morphology shows numerous canyon incisions. (2002) estimated that, on the Norwegian Sea margin, approximately 75% of sediment deposited in the deeper basins are provided by debris ﬂows. During interglacial times, contour currents driven by global thermohaline circulation have built a number of major sediment drifts (Laberg and Vorren, 2003b). These contourite drifts have been identiﬁed offshore Nor- way (Nyk drift, Dahlgren et al., 2002; Lofoten drift, Laberg and Vorren, 2003b), NW of Ireland (Feni drift, Haas et al., 2003) and offshore Shetlands and Faeroe (Van Weering et al., 1998a). Whereas contourite drifts in deep-sea basins south of 60�N are related to the circulation of deep-water masses (Mienert et al., 1994), drifts further north of 60�N on the Norwegian margin appear related to intermediate water masses (Laberg and Vorren, 2004). During glacial times, sedimentation rates on glaciated margins were high (several 10 m/kyr) and closely related to the location and dynamics of former ice streams (Sejrup et al., 2004). The last major phase of large-scale submarine sliding occurred during the Holocene, particularly offshore Norway (Storegga Slide, Trænadjupet Slide), where the geological history reveals long-term instability over the last 500 ka (Evans et al., 1996; Bryn et al, 2003; Haﬂidason et al., 2004; Solheim et al., 2005a). 2.2. Non-glaciated Atlantic margin between 35� and 52�N Between 35�N and 52�N, numerous submarine canyons incise the continental slope, thereby creating pathways for sediment transfer from the shelf break to the abyssal plains. The areas with canyons often have steep open slopes from 4� to 9�. The shelf width and thereby the distance to the sediment source area vary considerably. For example, the Porcupine margin (offshore Irish coast, approximately 52�N) and the Armorican margin (offshore French coast, 46�N) including the Celtic margin (48�N) are char- acterised by a relatively wide shelf (w150 km) which contrasts with the narrower shelf of the Iberian margin (from <10 km to 60 km). Sedimentation in the northern areas has been inﬂuenced by deglaciation and melt-water processes, but large-scale mass movements are scarce on this part of the margin (Weaver et al., 2000). Both the continental slope and rise are steep and narrow thus shortening the transport pathway from the shelf and upper slope to the abyssal plain. During glacial times and low sea levels, terrigenous sediment was delivered either directly to the canyon heads or at relatively short distances from the latter, which suggest higher transport activity within the canyons during these periods. Submarine fans developed at the outlet of the canyons and the wide-spread deposition from turbidity currents contributed to build-out the abyssal plains (Weaver et al., 2000). There are also important contourite systems on the non-glaciated margins, as for example in the Gulf of Cadiz and several sectors of the Mediterranean Sea (Rebesco and Stow, 2002). 2.2.2. Glaciated margins A list of documented submarine slope failures on the European glaciated margin north of 52�N is listed in Table 2. This table provides the database to assess the main parameters controlling slope failures on such margins. As mentioned above, the formerly glaciated margins are dominated by high sedimentation rates (1–40 m/kyr) related to the presence or proximity of an ice sheet and ice stream dynamics on the continental shelf during glacial times (e.g. Sejrup et al., 2004). The continental margins are also characterized by subsidence or uplift processes due to the existence or absence of ice sheets (Bungum et al., 2005). The margin is also swept by contour currents (Laberg and Vorren, 2004). 3.1.1. Triggering mechanisms: Seismic activity and seismic loading Seismic hazards offshore Fennoscandinavia (Fig. 1) might be underestimated considering the more pronounced seismic activity which likely followed the isostatic rebound from 10 ka to the present (Bryn et al., 2003; Bungum et al., 2005), seismic activity which was not observed to such a degree during the very recent period. Earthquake-induced excess pore pressure generation can lead to the liquefaction of coarse-grained, cohesionless soils. Therefore, a key question addresses the location, magnitude and frequency of earthquakes on these margins (Fig. 1), factors which can only be inferred from historical records or modelling scenarios for past times; this implies that uncertainty remains when relating the occurrence of certain slope failures with earthquakes. In general, one assumes that earthquakes are among the most obvious and best known triggering mechanisms for submarine slides (Piper et al., 1988). Depending on the direction of the earthquake-generated seismic waves, the seismic acceleration can increase the soil mass effect downslope and thus promote slope instability. However, another form of seismicity should be considered when discussing formerly glaciated margins, i.e. the seismicity related to glacio-isostatic processes. According to Siegert and Dowdeswell (2004), the Eurasian ice sheet reached its maximum volume of roughly 5.5 � 106 km3 around 16 ka. After the deglaciation, isostatic uplift has been estimated in the Barents Sea around 100 m/kyr at 9 ka and for Eastern Scandinavia around 300 m/kyr between 11 ka and 9 ka (Bungum et al., 2005). These authors proposed a fast uplift between 10 and 8 ka followed by a slower uplift between 7 and 2 ka. They also suggest that, while glacial isostatic adjustment and seismicity are related, the relationship is ambiguous. However, an intensiﬁed high seismicity period with the occurrence of several M 7þ earthquakes is documented at around 10 ka. Based on these results, they concluded that this was not enough to drastically affect the stability of this speciﬁc area. Kramer (1996) considered that slope stability is strongly inﬂu- enced by the strength resulting from large strains. Two types of strength should be considered: (1) the cyclic strength (during cyclic loading) that depends on both average shear stress and cyclic shear stress, and (2) the post-earthquake undrained shear strength that will be identical to the static case considering that no structural change takes place despite excess pore pressure development. However, the strength after cyclic loading can be reduced to about 40% with a peak cyclic strain equal to 75% of the failure strain in a static test. Hence, even a low cyclic strain can lead to a reduced post-earthquake strength and consequent slope failure. The dynamic behaviour (cumulative strain with repetitive cycles) can also reduce the soil’s shear resistance in non-cohesive sediments, and an earthquake-induced excess pore pressure generation can result in the liquefaction of sediments (Leynaud et al., 2004; Sultan et al., 2004a). 3.1.2. High sedimentation rates on the continental slope during ice ages (Sejrup et al., 2004) are another important factor in submarine slope stability assessment. Excess pore pressure development 3.1.2.2.1. Before complete consolidation. Rapid overloading of ﬁne-grained sediments could generate excess pore pressure depending on permeability and water content in the sediment. As the undrained shear strength of the sediment during the consoli- dation process depends on the excess pore pressure dissipation, the change in strength with time needs to be modelled. A high excess pore pressure developing in the soil during consolidation will impede the natural increase of effective stress with sediment burial. Depending on the excess pore pressure dissipation, the undrained shear strength might remain low. 3.1.2.2.2. After complete consolidation. When the sediment is initially fully consolidated (i.e. complete dissipation of excess pore pressure), a cyclic loading such as earthquake ground motion or gas accumulation can generate excess pore pressure in the sediment pores. The undrained shear strength is only affected by excess pore pressure generation if liquefaction occurs, or by cyclic loading leading to a possible degradation of shear strength. Therefore, the drained shear strength should be considered to ensure whether or not excess pore pressure conditions can result in slope failure. Bryn et al. Liquefaction of soils. Liquefaction of cohesionless soils is one process enhancing the likelihood of slope failures to occur. Liquefaction means that the excess pore pressure in sandy sedi- ments equals more or less the initial vertical effective stress (vertical effective stress becoming zero) and thus the sediment shear strength approaches null values (in other words, the sedi- ment behaves as a liquid). A sign of possible predisposing factor for a slope to fail was observed at the Afen slide (Fig. 1, No 13; Table 2). Wilson et al. (2003) observed the presence of well-sorted sands in debris lobes pointing towards the existence of formerly liqueﬁed layers. Contouritic sediments can act as weak layers considering their lower shear strength or higher sensitivity (Laberg et al., 2003), and they provide potential slip planes (Forsberg and Locat, 2005; Kvalstad et al., 2005a). Sandy contourites are even less cohesive and are susceptible to liquefy under dynamic loading (earthquakes). Consequently, such environmental changes may be responsible for the dissocia- tion of oceanic gas hydrates, releasing vast volumes of over- pressured gas and water in the conﬁned sediment’s pore space. This would ultimately affect the stability of the host sediments of gas hydrates (McIver, 1982; Kvenvolden, 1998). The effect environ- mental changes have on hydrate stability is complex: during glacial times, sea levels were typically several tens to up to 120 m lower than today (Fairbanks, 1989; Fleming et al., 1998), which would make hydrates less stable. However, during glacial times, the global ocean conveyor belt weakens, resulting in cold bottom water masses ﬂowing along the NE Atlantic continental margins (Dokken and Jansen, 1999). This would make hydrates more stable during glacial times. Consequently, one needs detailed information about the time scales and amplitudes of both sea level change and bottom water temperature ﬂuctuations before conclusions can be drawn about the environmental control on hydrate stability. This means, likewise, that the situation can be signiﬁcantly different from place to place, especially in the high-latitude areas presently enjoying warm water inﬂow. Creep, or secondary consolidation, corresponds to slow deformations with time at constant effective stress after the complete dissipation of excess pore pressure. Creep process occur on both glaciated and non-glaciated margins. This deformation results from the readjustment of particle contacts after the primary consolidation (Muir Wood, 1991). The creep process is summarized in Fig. 9 with the three different stages, with tertiary creep culmi- nating in failure. Okamoto et al. (2004) identiﬁed two recent landslides in Norway (in quick clay deposits) where secondary and tertiary creep stages were observed before the failure. 3.1.2.5.5. Slope steepening. Slope stability also depends on the dip angle as the downslope force increases with increasing dip. However, in most cases, enormous slides occurred on gentle slopes of less than 2 degrees (Hu¨hnerbach and Masson, 2004). This suggests that, locally, slope angle does not signiﬁcantly inﬂuence the occurrence of large-scale sliding on glaciated margins. High sedimentation rates and sea level changes. In contrast to the formerly glaciated NE Atlantic margin, the shelf of the Mediterranean Seas is relatively narrow. Only at the mouths of large rivers, well-deﬁned seaward prograding deltas have devel- oped. The most important ones are the Ebro, Rhone, Po and Nile deltas where sedimentation rates are typically high to very high with 10 cm/yr (100 m/kyr; Ambla`s et al., 2004). Average sedimen- tation rates around 2 m/kyr have been estimated on the upper slope in the Gulf of Lion (between 26 ka and 15 ka, Berne´ et al., 2004) but ‘‘instantaneous’’ rates can reach 1 m/yr in prodeltaic settings. According to Dubar and Anthony (1995) and L’homer (1980), an average sedimentation rate was estimated around 8 m/kyr between w12 ka and w7 ka (rapid sea level rise) and around 3.5 m/kyr between w7 ka and the present (slow sea level rise) for the Var delta. Discussion During the last 10–15 years, submarine mass movements and their consequences were more and more recognized as an impor- tant topic in continental margin research. In particular, the ques- tions about where, when, and why submarine mass movements occur are of prime interest (e.g. Locat and Mienert, 2003; Mienert, 2004) as well as the role of sea level changes driven by global climate change (e.g. Maslin et al., 2004). Low sea levels invoke changes in the local and global hydrodynamic regime and will affect gas hydrate stability. On glaciated margins during glacial times, the stability of submarine gas hydrates increased because cold bottom water masses present on the upper slope offsets the effect of pressure drop (Fig. 4). On non-glaciated margins, the stability of submarine gas hydrates probably decreased because warm water masses may prevail, while the pressure decreases (Maslin et al.,

climate change (e.g. Maslin et al., 2004). Low sea levels invoke changes in the local and global hydrodynamic regime and will affect gas hydrate stability. On glaciated margins during glacial times, the stability of submarine gas hydrates increased because cold bottom water masses present on the upper slope offsets the effect of pressure drop (Fig. 4). On non-glaciated margins, the stability of submarine gas hydrates probably decreased because warm water masses may prevail, while the pressure decreases (Maslin et al., 2004). Melting of hydrates results in excess pore pressure devel- opment, which is a key aspect for slope stability (Fig. 8). On non-glaciated margins, most submarine slope failures occurred between 45 ka and 16 ka (Maslin et al., 2004), which correspond to a low sea level-period (Fig. 11). The frequency of turbidites at those times was higher for the Horseshoe Abyssal Plain (Lebreiro et al., 1997). Sediment destabilization is most likely controlled by sediment supply, which in turn causes steeper slope angles. Periods of sea-level regression or transgression were proposed by Weaver et al. (1992) to correlate with large-volume turbidites rather than high or low sea-level stands. Marjanac, 1996 also suggested that the rate of sea level change could be the main factor to explain mega-beds deposition. Trincardi et al. (2003) speculate that two submarine slides on the Tyrrhenian margin (Paola and Licosa Slides) occurred in response to the relative sea- level rise or melt water pulse around 13.8 ka (20 m in 500 years). They noticed that the Big ’95 submarine slide dated around 11.5 ka also corresponds to a melt water pulse. A rise in sea level is accompanied by changes in the hydrody- namic and sedimentary regime. Additionally, the upper slopes of glaciated margins experience pronounced bottom water temperature increases during glacial–interglacial transitions. In contrast, non-glaciated margins were continuously submerged by warmer waters and should have experienced more stable gas hydrates due to sea level rise. The most important triggering mechanisms for slope failures on both glaciated and non-glaciated margins seem to be high magnitude earthquakes. Thus, both preconditioning factors and trigger mechanisms for causing slope failures existed during a very speciﬁc time period, i.e. the transition from glacial to interglacial time. In contrast, earth- quakes on active subduction zones of the Mediterranean margins can be considered to be frequent during both glacial and intergla- cial time. Here, the frequency of sliding appears more determined by preconditioning factors during glacial times. Rivers transported sandy sediments directly to the shelf edge and upper slope creating unstable slope conditions. The latter occurred during a low sea level when erosion by rivers caused major canyon incisions and mass movements on the upper slope as identiﬁed in the western Medi- terranean (e.g. Droz et al., 2001). 5. Conclusions According to the observations from glaciated and non-glaciated margins, one can draw the following conclusions concerning submarine slope instabilities. (1) From to the observed mass wasting types, we propose to split up the European continental margin in Glaciated (north of 52�N; presence of the ice cap during glacial period) and Non- Glaciated margin (south of 52�N). Large-scale slides dominate north of 62�N whereas megaturbidites and debris ﬂows are mainly observed south of 35�N. A broad range of mass wasting processes are observed in the Mediterranean sea whereas they are rather scarce between 35�N and 52�N on the Atlantic margin. (2) On glaciated margins (low slope angle), submarine slides are closely related to the extent of ice sheets and the location of con- tourites on continental slopes; north of 62�N, mega-scale sliding is preponderant during sea level rise from glacial to interglacial times whereas on non-glaciated margins (high slope angle), mega- turbidites and debris ﬂows occur predominantly during low sea level when rivers transported their sediment load directly to the shelf edge and coastal upwelling was limited to the upper slope. This suggests a relationship between the type of instabilities and the average slope angle of the continental margin; large-scale slides associated with low slope angles and presence of the ice sheet (role of excess pore pressure related to high sedimentation rates) while megaturbidites and debris ﬂows are rather associated with high slope angles and narrow shelf. (3) On glaciated margins, a combination of preconditions to failure exists during the Holocene such as excess pore pressure generation (from rapid deposition) with slow dissipation or gas hydrate dissociation. The ﬁnal triggering mechanisms are possibly high-magnitude earthquakes between 10 ka and 8 ka due to isostatic rebound during major ice sheet decay. Long-term insta- bility observed in the vicinity of the Storegga Slide (Glaciated margin) suggests a precondition to failure process related to recurrent glacial–interglacial period cycles. (4) Though the effect of excess pore pressure development on shear strength and subsequently slope failure is still not well understood, it appears that geotechnical properties of contourites play a major role in the instability mechanism on glaciated margins. Up until now, there is no sign of such inﬂuence of contourites on non-glaciated margins. (5) Non-glacigenic margins as presented experienced hal- okinetic processes and oversteepening of slopes, creating areas prone to failure. As these megaslides comprise two sets of stacked allochthonous masses within the Upper Miocene-Quaternary sedimentary record, they are now described as Mass-Transport Complexes (MTCs) and have been renamed the Amap�a Megaslide Complex (AMC) and the Par�a-Maranh~ao Megaslide Complex (PMMC). Individual megaslides of both MTCs can mobilize up to kilometre-thick sedimentary series as allochthonous masses with distinct ﬂow di- rections, degrees of sediment disruption and internal coherence. Megaslides spread downslope over areas as large as thousands of km2, attaining dimensions comparable to the world's largest mass- transport deposits. Among all the megaslides, the basal and largest AM1 megaslide (AMC) stands as a quite unique example of mass-transport deposit in the basin, interpreted as a dominant carbonate allochthonous mass sourced from a mixed carbonate-siliciclastic platform. The instability was probably triggered between the late Miocene and the end of the Early Pliocene by the gravitational collapse of the mixed platform under its own weight, after successive subaerial exposures which generated kar- stiﬁcation processes. Siliciclastic-type megaslides, on the other hand, are all sourced from large upslope slide and/or rotated blocks (up to 60 km wide in the case of the PMMC). The detachment of upslope blocks was triggered by structurally-induced seabed movements during the Mid Pliocene-Pleistocene (in the case of the PMMC) and during the Pleistocene (in the case of the AMC). Introduction The Foz do Amazonas basin (Amazon Mouth basin) is the largest offshore basin located on the Brazilian Equatorial Atlantic margin. This basin has been the target of systematic exploration by oil companies in recent decades, due to the potential occurrence of oil plays in the deep-water marine setting. The Amazon Deep-sea Fan (referred to hereinafter as the Amazon fan) stands as the main deep basin sedimentary feature, built out as a prominent, thick sedi- mentary prism, of about 10 km in thickness according to Brand~ao and Feij�o (1994) and Figueiredo et al. (2007). Mass-transport de- posits have also long been reported as important stratigraphic el- ements in the margin sedimentary construction, especially in the Upper Quaternary Amazon fan (e.g., Damuth and Embley, 1981; Damuth et al., 1988; Flood et al., 1991; Piper et al., 1997; Maslin et al., 2005). In most studies of the upper 500e800 m layers of the Amazon fan the occurrence of mass wasting has been correlated either with climate-induced processes, gas hydrate instability or sedi- ment loading (e.g., Damuth and Embley, 1981; Damuth et al., 1988; Flood et al., 1991; Piper et al., 1997; Maslin and Mikkelsen, 1997; Pirmez and Imran, 2003; Maslin et al., 2005). However, the Up- per Cretaceous to Quaternary stratigraphic section of the basin also glides along multiple d�ecollements in a linked extensional- compressional system (Cobbold et al., 2004; Silva et al., 2009; Reis et al., 2010). (2010), in order to clarify internal seismic facies, structures and the stratigraphy of the megaslides of both complexes. This procedure now provides the most detailed correlation framework with chronostratigraphic signiﬁcance for the Amap�a and the Par�a- Maranh~ao Megaslides. It has also allowed us to propose their source to sink processes as well as their main triggering mechanisms. 2. In terms of crus- tal structures, the Cear�a Rise stands as an outstanding aseismic ridge in the western Equatorial Atlantic located approximately 800 km east of the Amazon river mouth (Fig. 2). The top of this rise lies at about 3000 m below sea level, located just beyond the edge of the Amazon fan and surrounded by a seaﬂoor of an average depth of about 4500 m. The Amazon fan deposits lap onto the base of the western side of the Cear�a Rise at about 4200 m water depth (Curry et al., 1995; Dobson et al., 2001). The base of the stratigraphic succession of the Foz do Amazonas basin is composed of Neocomian to Albian ﬂuvio-deltaic, lacustrine and marine strata, inﬁlling pull-apart half-grabens (Brand~ao and Feij�o, 1994; Figueiredo et al., 2007). Open marine clastic deposi- tion started during the Eo-Albian (c. 102 Ma) with the deposition of deep-water mudstones and siltstones that lasted until the Neo- Paleocene (Limoeiro Formation; Fig. 3). The Cenozoic sedimentary history of the basin was dominated, from the late Paleocene to the late Miocene (~61.7e~9.5 Ma), by carbonates which were periodi- cally disrupted by siliciclastic deposition (Wolff and Carozzi, 1984; Gorini et al., 2014), resulting in the buildup of a mixed carbonate- siliciclastic platform as thick as 4000 m (Maraj�o and Amap�a For- mations), laterally equivalent to deep-water calcilutites and mud- stones (Travosas Formation; Fig. 3). The Cenozoic sedimentary history of the basin was dominated, from the late Paleocene to the late Miocene (~61.7e~9.5 Ma), by carbonates which were periodi- cally disrupted by siliciclastic deposition (Wolff and Carozzi, 1984; Gorini et al., 2014), resulting in the buildup of a mixed carbonate- siliciclastic platform as thick as 4000 m (Maraj�o and Amap�a For- mations), laterally equivalent to deep-water calcilutites and mud- stones (Travosas Formation; Fig. 3). During the development of the mixed carbonate-siliciclastic platform, the basin experienced a series of drowning phases intercalated with major regressive phases (Figueiredo et al., 2007). The last and most important drowning phase occurred during the Middle Miocene, reaching the maximum transgression during the Langhian (c. 15.2 Ma). Following this Middle Miocene maximum ﬂooding, coastal depositional systems prograded (Maraj�o Forma- tion; Fig. 3), while the carbonate platform continued to develop on the external continental shelf. This drowning phase lasted until the late Miocene when lower sea levels exposed, karstiﬁed and eroded the carbonate platform culminating in the deﬁnitive cessation of carbonate sedimentation at c. 9.5 Ma (Gorini et al., 2014). As recently shown by Gorini et al. (2014), until the late Pliocene increasing siliciclastic input into this basin occurred as dominantly prograding shelf clinoforms developed across the proximal basin, whereas higher siliciclastic input into deep-water settings occurred during the Quaternary. 2.1. Mass-transport deposits in the Foz do Amazonas Basin The upper 500e800 m of the Amazon fan (late Pleistocene) consist of channel-levee complexes interbedded with recurrent MTDs. Remobilized sediment masses (slumps, slides and debris ﬂows) can be as large as 15,000 km2, reaching individual thick- nesses of up to 200 m (e.g., Damuth and Embley, 1981; Damuth et al., 1988; Piper et al., 1997; Flood and Piper, 1997; Maslin et al., 2005), as occurs in (Fig. 1): the Western Superﬁcial Mass-Transport Deposits (WMTD), the Eastern Superﬁcial Mass-Transport Deposits (EMTD), the Unit R Mass-Transport Deposits (URMTD) and the Bot- tom Mass-Transport Deposits (BMTD). Gas hydrates destabilization, higher sedimentation rates during lowstands, and the rise of hydrostatic pressure during trans- gressions and sea-level highstands have been considered the main causes of slope instabilities and mass movement initiation for these Upper Pleistocene MTDs on the central Amazon fan (e.g., Damuth and Embley, 1981; Damuth et al., 1988; Flood and Piper, 1997; Piper et al., 1997; Maslin and Mikkelsen, 1997; Maslin et al., 2005). Slope morphology The morphology of the central Foz do Amazonas Basin is greatly affected by the Amazon fan deposition, whereas much steeper gradients are observed both on the NW and SE continental slopes adjacent to the fan, which are characterized by narrower conti- nental margins (Fig. 6). In the central basin, the gradient is rather subdued by the thick sedimentary sequences responsible for the Amazon fan's con- struction: the regional gradient on the upper fan is of the order of 0.9�; whereas on the middle fan the regional gradient is slightly smoother (of the order of 0.8�; proﬁle B in Fig. 6). On the other hand, the NW continental slope of the basin has the highest relative gradient values observed throughout the continental margin (up to 5.8�), followed by a reduction of gradient values from the depth of 2000 m basinwards (0.4e0.25�; proﬁle A in Fig. 6). The SE conti- nental slope of the basin is equally rather steep, presenting relative gradient values up to 4.0�, followed by a gradient reduction basinward from the depth of 3000 m (0.4�e0.5�; proﬁle C in Fig. 6). Triggering mechanisms Slope angle may have an important impact on slope instabilities but it is not the only indicator of susceptibility to landsliding (e.g., Migeon et al., 2006). Slope failure processes are generally triggered by a combination of several parameters, such as: oversteepening of the sea-ﬂoor, under-consolidated sediments and rapid sediment accumulation/sedimentary loading, which may generate an excess of pore pressure (e.g., Hampton et al., 1996; Biscontin and Pestana, 2006; Nisbet and Piper, 1998; Sultan et al., 2004a, 2004b; Canals et al., 2004; Bryn et al., 2005; Frey-Martinez et al., 2005; Frey- Martínez et al., 2006; Moscardelli et al., 2006; Migeon et al., 2006; Heinrich et al., 2008; Bull et al., 2009; Alves, 2010). Sudden and high amplitude sea level variations are also understood to be one of the causes for increasing pore pressure (e.g., Piper et al., 1997; Maslin and Mikkelsen, 1997; Maslin et al., 2004; Garziglia et al., 2008). SE ﬂanks of the Amazon fan, Foz do Amazonas basin. Our main results revealed that mass- transport processes have multiple implications for the basin's stratigraphic record, as well as for explotation strategies: (a) recurrent failure masses are recorded as large-scale MTCs, the Amap�a Megaslide Complex (AMC) and the Par�a- Maranh~ao Megaslide Complex (PMMC), involving individual volumes of allochthonous masses of up to c. 24,000 km3. Some of these failure masses are highly mobile and erosive, capable of travelling long downslope distances, which im- plies a great power of deformation and/or destruction of the original depositional architecture and stratigraphy of the basin; (b) successive subaerial exposures and karstiﬁcation processes of a mixed carbonate-siliciclastic platform favored its gravity collapse during the late Miocene-early Pliocene, generating a basal carbonate slide (AM1) which occurs only in the AMC, since it spreads out preferentially across the central- northwest basin, conditioned by the paleo bathymetry of the period; (c) most megaslides of these MTCs are siliciclastic in nature, sourced from sea-bed deformations generated by multistage rotation or the sliding of large upslope blocks (from 30 to 60 km wide). Blocks deformation was triggered by ﬂuid overpressure along a regional Upper Miocene condensed section, horizon H3, which also acts as the regional d�ecollement level for gravity tectonics in the basin; (d) ﬂuid overpressure conditions along H3 does not seem to have been attained synchronously throughout the basin. Submarine landslides and the importance of the initial sediment composition for run-out length and final deposit Anders Elverhoi & Hedda Breien & Fabio V. De Blasio & Carl B. Harbitz & Matteo Pagliardi Received: 28 April 2010 /Accepted: 2 July 2010 /Published online: 25 July 2010 # The Author(s) 2010. This article is published with open access at Springerlink.com Abstract Much remains to understand the dynamic processes during the flow of submarine landslides. A first relevant problem is to explain the extraordinary mobility of submarine landslides, which has no comparison in subaerial mass movement. Another challenging question is the apparent disparity between submarine landslides that remain compact for hundreds of kilometres and those that disintegrate during the flow, finally evolving into turbidity currents. This problem is linked to a central ongoing debate on the relative importance of turbidity currents versus submarine landslides in reshaping the continental margin. Based on three epitomic case studies and on laboratory experiments with artificial debris flows of various composition, we suggest a possible explanation for the disparity between compact and disintegrating landslides, identifying the clay-to-sand ratio as the key control parameter. submarine landslides may acquire extraordinary mobility. On the other hand, although the products of mass movement are easily recognised, the dynamic processes of submarine landsliding have never been observed in full scale. Moreover, in contrast to many subaerial landslides, submarine landslides are not accessible without costly oceanographic surveys. As a consequence, we know surprisingly little about the physical processes capable of transporting thousands of cubic kilometres of sediments for hundreds of kilometres along slopes that are only a fraction of a degree (e.g. Elverhoi et al. 2002; De Blasio et al. 2005; Breien et al. in press). A better understanding of submarine landsliding is also highly relevant for prediction of tsunamis (e.g. Harbitz et al. 1993). A prime question related to submarine landsliding regards the extraordinary mobility. Run-out ratios (i.e. fall height-to- travel distance) may reach values as low as 0.05–0.01 (De Blasio et al. 2006). This occurs on gentle slopes with inclination less than 1° in spite of an increased viscous drag and a reduced gravity due to buoyancy compared to subaerial conditions. A second key question is why some landslides remain compact during their flow while others disintegrate substantially, also developing into a bipartite flow with a high- and a low-density layer, commonly referred to as a high and a low-density turbidity current (e.g. Mulder and Cochonat 1996). The purpose of this paper is to use our most recent experimental flume results as background information in order to explain the apparent differences in the behaviour of three full-scale submarine landslides. Emphasis will be given on elucidating how the composition of the initially released masses may have influenced the flow behaviour and final deposition. Two of the landslides are well known and volumetrically huge, i.e. the Holocene Storegga landslide off western Norway (Solheim et al. 2005; Bryn et al. 2005) and the 1929 Grand Banks landslide off Nova Scotia/Newfoundland (e.g. Piper et al. 1999; Fig. 1a, b). In addition we focus on the Bear Island Fan complex, known for its late Pleistocene well-defined and long run-out debris flows (Laberg and Vorren 2000; Marr et al. 2002; Fig. 1a). It should be noted that in this paper, a debris flow has visco-plastic properties, while we apply the term ‘bipartite flow’ when the flow becomes completely fluidised and separates into a high- and a low-density layer, both with the properties of a Newtonian fluid (i.e. with zero yield strength). We thus restrict the term ‘fluidisation’ to a situation where the pore fluids obliterate the effect of particle friction. We also remark that in addition to cohesion, a debris flow may also include a frictional component in the rheology if not fully fluidised. The low- density layer corresponds to what is commonly referred to as the turbidity current, where ‘turbidity’ should refer to a certain low concentration of fine-grained particles in suspension as also proposed by Mulder and Alexander (2001), rather than the common interpretation of a turbulent regime. A significant part of the sediments consists of well-defined debris lobes. The lobes in the uppermost part of these sediments were most likely deposited during the last glacial maximum. They are typically about 30 m thick and 10 km wide, and comprised of clay-rich material (Laberg and Vorren 2000; Marr et al. 2002). The astonishing aspect of these debris flows is the enormous travel distance of more than 150 km despite an average seafloor inclination of only 0.7°, corresponding to a run-out ratio of only 0.012 (e.g. De Blasio et al. 2006). Seafloor mapping and sediment coring reveal rather homo- geneous composition along the whole flow path. Moreover, these debris flows do not seem to be associated with distal fine-grained deposits. It should also be noticed that a limited amount of erosion or erosional features have been related to the debris flows at the Bear Island Fan complex (e.g. Laberg and Vorren 2000). However, the Storegga landslide represents one major event (as opposed to the multi-flow system at the Bear Island Fan) with a first phase travelling more than 400 km and a termination phase dominated by a series of smaller landslides with significantly shorter travel distances of 10–15 km (Fig. 2). This might indicate disintegration of the debris flow and, as argued below, a possible transformation into a bipartite flow. 4 Laboratory experiments and sediment composition 4.1 Laboratory flume facility Flow experiments were performed at the St. Anthony Falls Laboratory, University of Minnesota, in a flume inside a 10-m long, 3-m high and 0.6-m wide tank (Fig. 3). The tank can be filled completely with water and has transparent Plexiglass walls. Inside the tank, the slope of a 0.2-m wide Plexiglass flume is adjusted to the desired inclination by means of wires. The flume bed has a layer of black roof shingle that provides an even degree of roughness of around 1 mm. At the top end of the flume, the debris flow slurry is filled into the head tank, which is opened by a gate mechanism. The gate is operated manually and automatically triggers the data acquisition system. The sediment runs down the inner flume and exits into the large tank at the end. The data acquisition system (Breien 2009) was synchronised, ensuring that all mea- surement sequences were triggered at the same instant when the gate was opened. Each camera recorded 4,000 frames per experiment, corresponding to 16.5 s. At a velocity of around 1 m/s, a frame rate of 240 fps would give a displacement of 25 pixels between two consecutive frames. In addition to the high-speed cameras, two standard digital- video cameras (PIXCI board cameras) were used to capture the overview (Fig. 3). A particle image velocimetry (PIV) algorithm (Sveen and Cowen 2004; Pagliardi 2007) applied to the high-speed camera images permitted us to calculate the velocity of the debris flow slurry particles close to the wall. We calculated the velocity field (u and v components) for each image, i.e. every 0.004 s and with a spatial resolution of about 1 mm, using cross-correlation methods between two sub-windows. Similar use of PIV can be found for example in Spinewine et al. (2003), Pouliquen (2004) and Barbolini et al. (2005). All three landslides originated from sediments provided from major ice sheets: (1) the Storegga landslide from the Fennoscandian ice sheet, (2) the Bear Island Fan landslides from the Barents Sea ice sheet and (3) the Grand Banks landslide from the Laurentian ice sheet. In principle, the sediment sources are similar, namely, glacially eroded prod- ucts, a situation likely to provide rather equal conditions and products. However, as documented from the three locations, the final deposits in the three sites differ strongly. In particular, extensive sand deposits on the abyssal plain similar to those associated with the Grand Banks landslide have not been found in connection with the other two landslides. As seen from the experiments, the primary composition plays an important role in the subsequent behaviour. Initial high clay content—or cohesive sediments—provides landslides that may remain as massive debris flows without disintegration. We suggest that a similar principle could occur for natural submarine debris flows. Because the Grand Banks landslide potentially had a more granular and less cohesive composition, we expect a lower critical shear stress for erosion compared to the Bear Island Fan complex (Fig. 13). In our interpretation, the Bear Island Fan complex corresponds to the clay-rich experiments, while the Grand Banks landslide is featured by more sand-rich experiments. The experiments reveal how the primary composition of the mobilised sediment (clayey versus sandy) determines the flow behaviour of submarine landslides. We conclude that clay-rich cohesive material, as found e.g. at the Bear Island Fan complex and in the Storegga landslide, may remain compact and attain extremely long run-out distances and high velocities on very gentle slopes in the ocean as a result of hydroplaning and acceleration of the head of the flow causing longitudinal extension of the entire body. If the sand content is increased, as e.g. in the Grand Banks landslide, the flow becomes less cohesive. on very gentle slopes in the ocean as a result of hydroplaning and acceleration of the head of the flow causing longitudinal extension of the entire body. If the sand content is increased, as e.g. in the Grand Banks landslide, the flow becomes less cohesive. This leads to internal particle segregation and a bipartite flow with the finer clay and silt forming an upper low-density layer, while the coarser material forms a lower sandy granular high- 1042 Ocean Dynamics (2010) 60:1027–1046 density layer. The process of particle segregation is a response to water intrusion and fluidisation and implies that the flow sprinkles sand on the seabed as it moves along, continuously loosing mass on its way and leaving behind a carpet of sand. This process also significantly reduces the erosive capability of the flow. Hydroplaning is still considered important to accelerate the frontal part of the debris flow to the velocities required for entrainment of particles from the head and frontal part of the debris flow, thus bringing particles into suspension and forming the upper low-density layer. Appendix Distorted scaling of subaqueous debris flows Idealised laboratory-scale experiments may not relate directly to the full-scale natural phenomenon. Hence, scaling aspects must be considered when performing such experiments. In many cases of interest, the flow dimensions can be scaled down in the model, while the dimensions of the microstructure (e.g. grain size) cannot. For instance, a sandy debris flow cannot be scaled down using clay instead of sand because the properties of cohesive material differ greatly from that of non-cohesive sand. In such cases, the link between field and laboratory is made through distorted geometric modelling in which the vertical and horizontal dimensions are scaled down by different amounts, as done by Graf (1971), Marr et al. (2001) and Mohrig and Marr (2003). Focussing on the rheological properties of the sediment (i.e. viscosity and yield strength), rather than grain size and interactions, circumvents the problem of scaling the microstructure. In practical terms, viscosity and yield strength may be reduced in the synthetic sediment by adding water to the slurry and reducing the clay content or using a different type of clay. As Eqs. 19 and 20 show, the slurry viscosity needs to be reduced. Both water and clay content will therefore usually need to be changed in going from field to laboratory scale. Care has to be taken that this does not significantly change the exponent α. We may conclude that, in general, flow regime transitions will not occur at the same clay content values at all scales. Moreover, different types of clay may induce different flow behaviour even with the same clay content, and this clay-type dependency may also be scale-dependent. Knight Keywords: Slope clinoform Sea-level variations Rollover trajectory 3D seismic Submarine landslide Three-dimensional (3D) seismic-reﬂection data has shed light on the character of a series of mass transport com- plexes (MTCs) emplaced during the Pleistocene in the Pescara Basin (Central Adriatic Sea, Italy). The Pescara Basin is the Plio-Pleistocene inner foredeep of the Central Apennines orogen, which was ﬁlled by a rapidly prograding, margin-scale clinoforms system. Three MTCs punctuate the normal turbiditic and hemipelagic sed- imentary succession of the Pescara Basin foredeep. MTC_0 is the oldest one and covers an area of around 74 km2. It is composed of three different mass transport deposits (MTDs) resulting from individual collapses that in- volved a shelf-edge delta during a period of relative sea level rise. MTC_1, the intermediate age MTC, is the largest one, with an area of 90 km2. It has a 10 km wide cookie-bite headwall region that indents the upper slope and, in places, reaches the continental shelf-break. MTC_1 is made up of four laterally and vertically stacked MTDs which are the result of a composite set of failures that migrated progressively upslope in a sedimentary setting domi- nated by contourite deposits. Its geo- morphic setting leads us to consider two different episodes of failure rooted at different depths. The investigation of the MTCs, through the coupling of 3D seismic geomorphology, seismic facies analysis and rollover trajectory analysis, reveals that the type of sedimentary environment, the rate of sediment accumu- lation, the source region and the depth of rooting of the failure, are the major controlling factors on MTC evo- lution and emplacement. Each MTC of the Pescara Basin foredeep is generally conﬁned within a discrete clinotheme. Finally, the rollover trajectory analysis has shown that, in the PB foredeep, a sediment failure can possibly occur at any relative sea level position. © 2013 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved. 1. Introduction Multibeam bathymetric and subsurface 2D/3D seismic surveys are revealing that the deposits of catastrophic mass transport events (MTEs) are important constituents of continental margins worldwide. The awareness that MTEs play a crucial role in reshaping continental margins and in controlling the architecture of sedimentary basin ﬁlls, has also prompted the interest of the hydrocarbon industry (Mulder and Cochonat, 1996; Frey-Martinez et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2007; Bull et al., 2008; Moscardelli and Wood, 2008; Shipp et al., 2011). The sed- imentary product of a single MTE is named a Mass Transport Deposit (MTD). The results of more than one MTE are composite depositional bodies that are called Mass Transport Complexes (MTCs) (Weimer, 1989; Frey-Martinez et al., 2005; Moscardelli and Wood, 2008). For a long time MTCs have been largely ignored by the oil industry as they were considered as unattractive reservoir targets (Weimer and Slatt, 2004). However, more recently, the importance of MTCs for oil exploration and exploitation has been recognized (Posamentier and Kolla, 2003; Garziglia et al., 2008). MTEs along continental margins can transfer shelf-edge and upper slope sandy sediments toward the base of slope and basin ﬂoor environments giving rise to an accu- mulation of potential reservoir lithology (Meckel et al., 2011). Fur- thermore, MTCs ﬁlled with locally overpressured gas or water in the shallow subsurface can represent a geohazard during drilling opera- tions and during pipeline implementation (McLeod and Underhill, 1999; Weimer and Slatt, 2004; Urgeles et al., 2007). Earthquakes, slope over-steepening, rapid sediment accumulation, gas hydrate dissociation, groundwater seepage, stormwave loading and sea-level ﬂuctuations are considered the main triggers for MTE gen- eration (Locat and Lee, 2002; Masson et al., 2006). The morphology and the degree of internal deformation of a MTC are mainly controlled by the rheology of the sed- iment involved, the gradient of the slope and the degree of conﬁnement of the basin (Lucente and Pini, 2003; Frey-Martinez et al., 2005). There- fore, geomorphologic classiﬁcations are not merely descriptive but are often used to reconstruct kinematic models for MTC emplacement (Frey-Martinez et al., 2005; Gee et al., 2006; Bull et al., 2008; Moscardelli and Wood, 2008). Geomorphologic classiﬁcation divides the sediment failure into various domains: the “evacuation zone” en- compasses the landslide failure headwall scar, which is generally dom- inated by extensional and erosional processes; the “translational zone” which comprises the sector where the failed sediments, are translated downslope; and the “accumulation zone”, i.e. the region where the bulk of the failed sediments is found and where contractional strain prevails. The “toe region” represents the down slope termination of any MTD/MTC. In this study, through the interpretation of industrial 3D seismic data, we present three MTCs from the Pleistocene slope clinoform suc- cession of the Pescara Basin (PB), the Plio-Pleistocene inner foredeep of the Central Apennines (Fig. 1). A qualitative 3D seismic geomorphology analysis has been coupled with the “classical” 2D seismic facies analysis with the aim of reconstructing the MTCs geomorphology and the char- acter of their source areas. The focus of our approach is to decipher the sedimentary setting of the PB foredeep and to pinpoint the source sed- imentary environment of each MTC. With this in mind, 3D seismic geo- morphology techniques have been used to generate a series of attribute maps in order to recognize the internal geometries and the architecture of each MTC. The same approach has been applied to recognize the ele- mentary MTDs composing each MTC.

The investigated portion of the PB sedimentary succession consists of a series of mud-dominated, eastward-dipping clinoforms which have developed since the Plio-Pleistocene (Dalla Valle et al., 2012) (Fig. 1B). The slope clinoforms have thicknesses ranging from 350 m to 500 m (Dalla Valle et al., 2012). The development of the slope clinoforms was not affected by syn-sedimentary tectonic activity that halted during the deposition of pre-Pliocene sediments (Fig. 2). The MTCs discussed in this study are buried at depths ranging from 1000 m to 350 m below the seaﬂoor of the Adriatic Sea (Fig. 2B, C). 3. Material and methods The total coverage of the 3D seismic data sets amounts to 1600 km2, extending offshore of the Central Adriatic Sea (Fig. 2). The seismic data were migrated with a single pass 3D post-stack time migration with a 2 ms sampling interval, processed to near-zero phase. Data are displayed using SEG normal polarity, where an increase in acoustic im- pedance is represented by a high-amplitude peak (white reﬂector in the selected color bar). The 3D volume, at the considered depths, has a dominant frequency of 60 Hz, with an estimated vertical resolution of around 20 m at an average interval velocity of 1800 m/s. In particular, we have used a semblance attribute, which is a math- ematical measure of similarity between two or more windowed seismic traces. The semblance attribute can be used to denote lateral changes in seismic response caused by lithologic and structural variability and hydrocarbon proprieties. Sweetness is an attribute used for identifying sands or coarse-grained sediments and is derived by combining instan- taneous frequency and reﬂection strength (Radovich and Oliveros, 1998). Description and interpretation of mass transport complexes (MTCs) Three large scale MTCs, buried at different depths, have been rec- ognized in the Pleistocene sedimentary succession of the PB foredeep (Fig. 2). The criteria for the distinction of the MTCs are based on the recognition of km-scale sedimentary bodies characterized by seismic facies made up of highly discontinuous to chaotic reﬂectors (Fig. 2). At their base, MTCs are generally bound by a high-amplitude reﬂector that truncates otherwise laterally continuous units (Fig. 2). Based on differences in overall internal and external geometry, on seismic fa- cies variability and on stratigraphic termination of their bounding re- ﬂectors, we have also recognized the elementary MTDs composing each MTC (Figs. 4, 6, 8). Due to seismic resolution, only individual bodies with a minimum thickness of around 20/25 m can be mapped separately. Discussion The study performed in the Pescara Basin foredeep has permitted the recognition of three large scale MTCs and the identiﬁcation of sedimentary scenarios of their source regions at the time of failure. The integration of 3D seismic geomorphology techniques and rollover- trajectory analysis has allowed us to recognize repeated margin collapses 133 G. Source sedimentary environments We can recognize three main sedimentary settings that are dis- tinctively affected by MTCs in the Pescara Basin foredeep: shelf- edge deltas, contouritic drifts and open slope bulges. It appears, with- in the limits of the seismic resolution, that the stratal architecture, in each setting, dictates the depth of detachment and the volume of the failed material. Despite the stratigraphic architectural setting that controls the pre-conditioning factors, external perturbations such as sudden cyclic loading by earthquakes, are likely to be the main trig- gering factor for the failures for all of the MTCs of the PB foredeep in this seismically active terrain. 5.1.1. Failure of the shelf-edge delta MTC_0 has been generated by a series of MTEs that have involved a shelf-edge delta system and thus, we classify MTC_0 as a shelf-attached system (sensu Moscardelli and Wood, 2008). MTC_0 develops within a clinotheme that shows a marked delta progradation, resulting in a perched sedimentary wedge in the shelf toward the upper slope sector (Figs. 3B, 4A). In the MTC_0 case, high sedimentation rates have promoted the delta progradation toward the shelf-edge and the upper-slope, with the creation of a shelf-perched wedge-shaped body in the upper slope. In this setting, high sedimentary accretion could have promot- ed the formation of high pore water pressure within the delta sedi- ments, thus generating instability. The excess pore water pressure resulting from high sedimentation rate or seismic loading linked to an earthquake are generally considered the main triggering mecha- nism for failure of submarine deltas (Lee et al., 2007; Sultan et al., 2010). The instability of shelf-edge deltas, resulting in large scale MTCs, has been documented worldwide in a variety of geodynamic settings (Porebski and Steel, 2003; Nelson et al., 2011). Failures of deltaic deposits have been largely documented in modern examples, such as in the Var delta (Sultan et al., 2010), in the Magdalena delta (Romero-Otero et al., 2010), in the Nile delta (Garziglia et al., 2008) and in the Gulf of Mexico (Perov and Bhattacharya, 2011). Furthermore, the formation of biogenic gas resulting from the de- position and decay of organic matter can lead to high pore water pressure with a consequent state of extreme under-consolidation of the delta sediments. The role of gas charged sediment acting as a preconditioning factor has been proposed for the Holocene failures in the Lower St.

Magdalena delta (Romero-Otero et al., 2010), in the Nile delta (Garziglia et al., 2008) and in the Gulf of Mexico (Perov and Bhattacharya, 2011). Furthermore, the formation of biogenic gas resulting from the de- position and decay of organic matter can lead to high pore water pressure with a consequent state of extreme under-consolidation of the delta sediments. The role of gas charged sediment acting as a preconditioning factor has been proposed for the Holocene failures in the Lower St. Lawrence Estuary (Cauchon-Voyer et al., 2008) and for mass transport deposits found in the western Nile delta (Garziglia et al., 2008). 5.1.2. Failure of sediment drift deposits The MTEs which have generated MTC_1 have affected the continen- tal slope, reaching the shelf-break region locally (Fig. 7A). Therefore, MTC_1 is classiﬁed as a slope-attached MTC (sensu Moscardelli and Wood, 2008). The seismic facies of mounds, drifts and large-scale mudwaves growing along inclined surfaces of the slope surrounding MTC_1 indicates a sedimentary environment shaped by bottom cur- rents generating contourite deposits (Fig. 7A). Sedimentary instability of contourite deposits is documented along continental slopes worldwide, playing a key role in the largest known MTCs such as the Storegga and Trænadjupet slides, offshore Norway (Laberg et al., 2002; Solheim et al., 2005). Examples of fail- ures of contourite deposits have also been documented in the Medi- terranean area, especially along the southwestern Adriatic Margin (Verdicchio and Trincardi, 2008), in the Gela Basin foredeep (Minisini and Trincardi, 2009), and in the Gulf of Cadiz (Mulder et al., 2003). Contourite deposits are generally characterized by high sedimentation rates and highwater content which are among the predisposing factors that concur to the lowering of the sediment shear strength (Sultan et al., 2004; Laberg and Camerlenghi, 2008). 5.1.3. It develops in correspondence with a marked depositional bulge on the slope (Fig. 8C, D). The high-aggradational component of the clinotheme, both on the shelf and on the slope-basin ﬂoor, reﬂects an increased sedimentary accumulation rate in this speciﬁc portion of the PB (Fig. 8C, D). Such a local high rate of deposition may be due to a direct ﬂuvial input or sediment redistribution along the PB margin. On the shelf, no evi- dence of deltas or incised valleys has been documented, and the slope is featureless, showing only draped conduits like canyons and slope channels (Fig. 8C). MTD_0.1 has involved the upper slope region and probably also the shelf-break region (Fig. 9A). In our interpretation, the MTE has left a post-failure depression in the slope facing the shelf-edge delta, that has been carved by successive sediment gravity ﬂows forming the slope chutes (Fig. 9A). The accumulation zone of MTD_0.1 is dominat- ed by pressure ridges, frontal ramps and slabs of sediment ripped up from the basal shear-surface. The presence of a counter-slope sector, linked to the presence of a healed structural high buried below the distal ac- cumulation zone of MTD_0.1 can be responsible for these observed syn-depositional, contractional features (Fig. 4A). Failures at any sea level stage While classical sequence-stratigraphy models consider that MTEs occur preferably during sea level lowstands, a wide number of studies carried out on passive and active continental margins have shown that MTCs can also occur during sea level rise and high-stand periods (Laberg et al., 2002; Maslin et al., 2004; Haﬂidason et al., 2005; Locat et al., 2009; Twichell et al., 2009). In the PB foredeep, the lack of accurate dating hampers a calibra- tion of the emplacement of the different MTCs with relative sea level cycles. Nevertheless, along continental margins characterized by a lack of large tectonic deformation, and by steady subsidence, roll- over trajectory analysis can be used as an indicator of relative sea level trend (Helland-Hansen and Hampson, 2009). By examining the long-term trends of rollover trajectory of the clinothemes enclosing the studied MTCs it can be stated that in the PB foredeep, MTEs occur during different rollover point trajectories and thus during different relative sea level positions (Fig. 10). MTC_0 is enclosed within a clinotheme that shows an ascending trajectory of the rollover points consistent with a rise of relative sea level (Fig. 10A). MTC_1, on the other hand, is enclosed within a clinotheme with a slightly descending rollover trajectory which cor- responds with a progressive lowering of the relative sea level (Fig. 10B). On the contrary MTC_2 is enclosed within a clinotheme with a high-angle ascending rollover trajectory, with a high aggrada- tion acting along the whole clinotheme (Fig. 10C). This evidence indi- cates that MTC_2 affected the slope during a relative sea level rise and/or high stand

Taking into ac- count these markedly different conditions of the relative sea level during each MTC emplacement, we may assume that the failure events are controlled by the depositional environment rather than by relative sea level. In particular, in the PB foredeep the sedimentary setting represents the major factor that promotes sediment failure. Our study shows that failures affect the areas of high sedimentation rates in each depositional environment. 5.4. MTCs and clinothemes The MTCs documented in the study area display signiﬁcant differ- ences in the internal architecture, external morphology, nature of the de- posits involved and timing of formation relative to inferred sea level change. However, despite all these differences, all the MTEs share a major characteristic: each time a MTE occurs, it affects only one clinotheme. Each MTD is a relatively extensive but “thin skinned” deposit (typically less than 80 m) generated at the expense of one progradational margin-clinotheme and may form either at the shelf-edge or in the slope. This evidence indicates that the main predisposing factor for sediment failure in this area is always a time interval of increased accumulation rate on the margin and that permeability barriers and lithological changes within the stratal architecture maintain each failure event some- what

Conclusions The MTCs of the PB foredeep, investigated through a 3D geomor- phological approach coupled with a 2D seismic facies analysis and rollover trajectory analysis, have revealed that: • MTEs can occur at any sea level position; the sea level does not ap- pear to act as a triggering mechanism in this framework. • The morphology of the MTC reﬂects the stratigraphy of the failed sec- tion and their source sedimentary environment (i.e., subaqueous delta, contouritic deposit, advection-dominated open slope depocenter). • The sediment failures are always conﬁned within a discrete clinotheme. The depth of rooting of each MTD is a further important controlling factor in the resultant deposit morphology, even within the same mass transport complex. In the PB foredeep, the main predisposing factor for the MTEs ini- tiation is represented by a major increase in accumulation rate along the margin, which can occur irrespective of sea level variations. text: Interactions between submarine channel systems and deformation in deepwater fold belts: Examples from the Levant Basin, Eastern Mediterranean sea Ian R. Clark*, Joseph A. Cartwright School of Earth and Ocean Sciences, Cardiff University, Main building, Park Place, Cardiff, CF10 3YE, United Kingdom a r t i c l e i n f o Article history: Received 20 May 2008 Received in revised form 11 May 2009 Accepted 22 May 2009 Available online 23 June 2009 Keywords: Channel levee systems Sediment–structure interactions Nile delta Salt tectonics 3D seismic a b s t r a c t Submarine channel levee systems form important hydrocarbon reservoirs in many deep marine settings and are often deposited within a structurally active setting. This study focuses on recent submarine channels that developed within a deepwater fold and thrust belt setting from the Levant Basin, eastern Mediterranean Sea. Compressional deformation within the study area is driven by the up-dip collapse of the Nile cone above the ductile Messinian Evaporites. Structures such as folds and strike slip faults exert a strong control on channel location and development over time. From this study four end-member submarine channel–structure interactions can be deﬁned: Conﬁnement, diversion, deﬂection and blocking. Each of these channel–structure interactions results in a distinct submarine channel morphology and pattern of development compared to unconﬁned channel levee systems. Each interaction can also be used to assess timing relationships between submarine channel development and deformation. � 2009 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved. 1.
